rows.longest_span: a complete accurate concise and clear record of the audit including
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.5.1 covers preparing the audit report, which provides a complete, accurate, concise and clear record of the audit including its scope, criteria, findings and conclusions.

rows.longest_span: based on the seven outlined in 4 2 to 4 8
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 presents the seven principles without ranking them: clause 4.1 says only that adherence to them is fundamental, and that Clauses 5 to 7 are based on the seven outlined in 4.2 to 4.8. It states nothing about precedence in either direction - the words precedence, hierarchy and rank do not appear in the document. Where two principles engage a situation differently, nothing in the text decides between them and the auditor weighs them.

rows.longest_span: the communication should be truthful accurate objective timely clear and complete
rows.description: The fair presentation principle in ISO 19011:2026 clause 4.3 says audit findings, conclusions and reports should reflect the auditing activities truthfully and accurately, and that the communication should be truthful, accurate, objective, timely, clear and complete. Like every principle in clause 4 it is expressed as a should, not a shall - ISO 19011 is a guidance document and contains no requirements. The statement records what was found; it does not prescribe the remedy or characterise the auditee.

rows.longest_span: the audit team becomes aware of new or changed circumstances or
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.4.7 records that where the audit team becomes aware of new or changed circumstances, or of risks or opportunities, these should be addressed accordingly. A plan is a design, not a commitment to ignore what the evidence shows. Changes are agreed with the audit client and auditee and recorded, so that the report describes the audit that was actually conducted.

rows.longest_span: to the audit plan introduce the audit team and their roles
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.4.3 covers the opening meeting, whose purpose is to confirm the agreement of all parties to the audit plan, introduce the audit team and their roles, and ensure that the planned activities can be performed. Its degree of formality varies with the type of audit; for a routine internal audit it can be simply communicating that the audit is being conducted and explaining its nature.

rows.longest_span: should not influence or interfere with the conduct of the audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.4.2 covers assigning the roles and responsibilities of guides and observers. A guide accompanies the audit team, arranges access and interviews and provides clarification; an observer attends without auditing. Neither acts as an auditor, and the presence of either should not influence or interfere with the conduct of the audit.

rows.longest_span: that relevant interested parties can have requirements related to climate change
rows.description: Clause 4.2 carries a note recording that relevant interested parties can have requirements related to climate change. It is a note, which makes it neither a requirement nor guidance in the sense a should carries, and no finding can be raised on it. It signals where the topic can surface when interested-party requirements are determined.

rows.longest_span: ai management system performance including trends in nonconformities and corrective actions
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.3.2 requires the management review to include, among its inputs, information on AI management system performance including trends in nonconformities and corrective actions, in monitoring and measurement results, and in audit results. Internal audit output is therefore not an end in itself: it is a named input to the review, and a management review record that does not reflect audit results leaves that element of 9.3.2 unevidenced.

rows.longest_span: include access to adequate and appropriate information and communication technology
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.4.4 covers determining programme resources, which include access to adequate and appropriate information and communication technology.

rows.longest_span: responsibilities and authorities for relevant roles are assigned and communicated
rows.description: Clause 5.3 requires top management to ensure responsibilities and authorities for relevant roles are assigned and communicated, and to assign authority for ISMS conformity and for reporting performance to top management.

rows.longest_span: the changes shall be carried out in a planned manner
rows.description: Clause 6.3 requires that where the organization determines the need for changes to the ISMS, the changes shall be carried out in a planned manner. It does not appear on the standard's own contents page, which is how it is routinely missed.

rows.longest_span: an inventory of information and other associated assets including owners
rows.description: Identifying AI tools in use within scope that did not pass through procurement, change control or the asset inventory, and which therefore appear in no ISMS record. Annex A 5.9 requires an inventory of information and other associated assets including owners.

rows.longest_span: internal audit the audit client can also be the auditee
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.13 defines the audit client as the organization or person requesting the audit, and clause 3.14 defines the auditee as the organization or the parts of it being audited. A note to 3.13 records that in an internal audit the audit client can also be the auditee, or the individual managing the audit programme. The roles stay distinct even when one organization fills all of them, and identifying who requested the audit is how the auditor knows to whom the report is owed.

rows.longest_span: the ability to make reasoned judgements in all audit situations
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 4.4 describes due professional care as the application of diligence and judgement in auditing, and names the ability to make reasoned judgements in all audit situations as an important factor in exercising it. Because the document offers guidance rather than requirements, and because it ranks no principle above another, the resolution of a genuine tension is the auditor's reasoned judgement rather than a rule the auditor can cite. Annex A.3 gives further guidance on professional judgement.

rows.longest_span: and present them to the audit client when developing the
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.3 records that risks and opportunities related to the auditee's context can affect the achievement of the audit programme's objectives, and that the individual managing the programme should identify them and present them to the audit client when developing the programme and its resource requirements. The clause lists risk sources including planning, resources, selection of the audit team, communication, implementation, records and their control, and monitoring and review. These are risks to the audit, not the auditee's own risks.

rows.longest_span: generally includes a description of the physical and virtual locations
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.6 defines audit scope as the extent and boundaries of an audit, with a note that it generally includes a description of the physical and virtual locations, functions, organizational units, activities and processes, and the time period covered. For an AI management system audit the virtual locations and the specific AI systems in scope matter as much as the organizational units, and a scope that names neither cannot later be tested against a finding.

rows.longest_span: information provides sufficient objective evidence that requirements are being met
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.5 asks the auditor to consider, so far as practicable, whether information provides sufficient objective evidence that requirements are being met: whether it is complete, meaning all expected content is present; correct, meaning it conforms to other reliable sources; consistent, in itself and with related documented information; and current. It adds that where information arrives in a manner other than expected, the integrity of the audit evidence should be assessed.

rows.longest_span: be held with individuals from appropriate levels and functions performing
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.17 a) asks that interviews be held with individuals from appropriate levels and functions performing the activities or tasks within the audit scope. For an AI management system this means the people who actually prepare data, evaluate models or operate the system, not only the manager who can describe the intended process. Interviewing only upward produces a description of the design rather than evidence of the practice.

rows.longest_span: the scope and complexity of the audit and can include
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.14 addresses selecting sources of information, which vary with the scope and complexity of the audit and can include interviews, observation, documented information, records, data summaries and reports from other sources. The choice follows from the question being asked: a summary answers a different question from the record it summarises.

rows.longest_span: responsibilities and authorities for relevant roles are assigned and communicated
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 5.3 requires top management to ensure responsibilities and authorities for relevant roles are assigned and communicated, and specifically to assign responsibility and authority for ensuring the AIMS conforms to the requirements of the standard and for reporting on its performance to top management. A note points to control A.3.2 for defining and allocating AI roles and responsibilities.

rows.longest_span: with those in annex a to verify that no necessary
rows.description: Clause 6.1.3 b) requires the organization to determine all controls necessary to implement the chosen treatment options and to compare them with those in Annex A to verify that no necessary control has been omitted. The direction matters: controls are determined from the risks first and Annex A is then used as a completeness check. An organization that started from Table A.1 and worked backwards has performed a different exercise, and the audit evidence for the comparison is what shows which happened.

rows.longest_span: exercise discretion in the use and protection of information acquired
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 4.5 asks auditors to exercise discretion in the use and protection of information acquired during auditing, including proper handling of sensitive or confidential information. This can pull against the completeness that clause 4.3 asks for, particularly where evidence includes personal data or commercially sensitive model details. Nothing in the text ranks the two, and the usual resolution is to state the finding fully while holding the underlying evidence in the audit record rather than the distributed report.

rows.longest_span: define the audit criteria and scope for each audit
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 9.2.2 a) requires the organization to define the audit criteria and scope for each audit. It does not require audit objectives. ISO/IEC 42001's own 9.2.2 a) adds objectives where ISO/IEC 27001 does not.

rows.longest_span: be available as documented information communicated within the organization
rows.description: Clause 5.2 separately requires the policy to be available as documented information, communicated within the organization, and available to interested parties as appropriate.

rows.longest_span: to annex a to ensure that no necessary controls
rows.description: NOTE 2 to clause 6.1.3 directs users to Annex A to ensure that no necessary controls are overlooked; NOTE 3 states the listed controls are not exhaustive. Annex A verifies nothing was missed; it is not a catalogue to select from.

rows.longest_span: analysed and evaluated and who shall analyse and evaluate
rows.description: Clause 9.1 requires the organization to determine six things: what needs monitoring and measuring including processes and controls, the methods, when performed, who shall monitor and measure, when results are analysed and evaluated, and who shall analyse and evaluate.

rows.longest_span: fulfilment of information security objectives feedback from interested parties
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 9.3.2 additionally requires fulfilment of information security objectives, feedback from interested parties, and risk assessment results and treatment plan status. ISO/IEC 42001 requires none of these three. Carrying the 27001 list into a 42001 audit raises findings that are not requirements.

rows.longest_span: requirements for auditing management systems for third party certification
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Table 1 separates audits by who requests and who conducts them. First party is the internal audit an organization performs on itself. Second party is an audit of an external provider, or an audit of the organization by an external interested party. Third party covers certification audit, accreditation assessment, and statutory or regulatory audit. The document states in its introduction that it concentrates on first and second party, and that ISO/IEC 17021-1 provides the requirements for auditing management systems for third-party certification.

rows.longest_span: one another to reach similar conclusions in similar circumstances
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 4 sets out seven principles: integrity (4.2), fair presentation (4.3), due professional care (4.4), confidentiality (4.5), independence (4.6), evidence-based approach (4.7) and risk-based approach (4.8). Clause 4.1 states that adherence to them is fundamental to audit conclusions that are relevant and sufficient, and that it enables auditors working independently of one another to reach similar conclusions in similar circumstances. Each principle is expressed as a should.

rows.longest_span: requirements may include policies procedures work instructions legal requirements
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.8 defines audit criteria as the set of requirements used as a reference against which objective evidence is compared. A note records that requirements may include policies, procedures, work instructions, legal requirements and contractual obligations, and a further note that where the criteria are legal requirements the words compliance and non-compliance are often used in a finding. For this credential the criteria are ISO/IEC 42001:2023 together with the organization's own AI management system requirements, as clause 9.2.1 of that standard sets out.

rows.longest_span: requirements for auditing management systems for third party certification
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 states in its introduction that ISO/IEC 17021-1 provides the requirements for auditing management systems for third-party certification, and that ISO 19011 can offer useful additional guidance alongside it. ISO/IEC 17021-1 governs the certification body, not the organization being audited and not its internal auditors. Concepts an internal auditor may meet from that world, such as a major and minor grading of nonconformities, originate there rather than in ISO/IEC 42001.

rows.longest_span: determine external and internal issues relevant to its purpose
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 4.1 requires the organization to determine external and internal issues relevant to its purpose, to consider the intended purpose of the AI systems it develops, provides or uses, and to determine its roles with respect to those systems. This is a requirement of the standard and the determination is auditable: the auditor looks for the systems named, the roles assigned and the reasoning recorded.

rows.longest_span: technology during the audit process for observing interviewing and
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.16 addresses remote auditing methods: an audit using technology during the audit process for observing, interviewing and verifying objective evidence. It records that remote methods can be necessary for auditing virtual locations, that ensuring the audit is effectively conducted is a joint responsibility of auditee and auditors, and that remote methods can introduce additional risks and opportunities. The fourth edition expanded this guidance from ISO/IEC TS 17012.

rows.longest_span: the reason for the interview and any note taking
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.17 asks that the reason for the interview and any note taking be explained, and that the results be summarised and reviewed with the interviewee. Confirming the record at the time is what allows a statement of fact to be relied on later, and it protects the interviewee from a finding built on something they did not mean.

rows.longest_span: limited feasibility of non verbal communication in virtual settings
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.17 f) asks that the type of question be carefully selected, naming open, closed, leading questions and appreciative inquiry, and A.17 g) notes the limited feasibility of non-verbal communication in virtual settings, directing attention instead to the type of question used to find objective evidence. A leading question produces agreement rather than information, and agreement is not evidence.

rows.longest_span: information is provided in a manner other than expected
rows.description: A screen share shows what the person operating it chose to display, at the moment they displayed it. That can be genuine evidence of a control operating, and it can equally be a filtered view or a prepared environment. Annex A.5 asks that where information is provided in a manner other than expected, the integrity of the audit evidence be assessed; recording what was actually observed, and by whom it was navigated, is how the auditor keeps that assessment possible.

rows.longest_span: diverging opinions between the audit team and the auditee
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.4.10 covers the closing meeting, at which the audit findings and conclusions are presented so that they are understood and acknowledged. It is where diverging opinions between the audit team and the auditee are discussed and, where possible, resolved, and where any unresolved difference is recorded rather than smoothed over.

rows.longest_span: additional controls are necessary beyond those in annex a
rows.description: Clause 6.1.3 d) requires the organization to identify whether additional controls are necessary beyond those in Annex A, and Annex A.1 records that the organization can design and implement its own controls. Annex A is a reference set and not a ceiling. A statement of applicability containing only Table A.1 rows is not automatically deficient, but it does invite the question of whether step d) was performed.

rows.longest_span: implement the controls determined according to 6 1 3
rows.description: A statement of applicability records what the organization decided. Implementation evidence shows what it did. Clause 8.1 requires the organization to implement the controls determined according to 6.1.3, so a control declared as included and not implemented is a nonconformity against clause 8.1 rather than against Table A.1. Reading only the statement of applicability tests the decision and not the operation.

rows.longest_span: actions are usually decided and undertaken by the auditee
rows.description: Deciding how to correct a nonconformity belongs to the auditee. ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.7 records that corrections and corrective actions are usually decided and undertaken by the auditee. An auditor who writes the fix into the finding has made the auditee's decision for them and has also made the finding harder to close, because it can now be satisfied only one way.

rows.longest_span: dealing with audit findings related to multiple criteria where
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.18.4 addresses dealing with audit findings related to multiple criteria, where a single body of evidence bears on requirements from more than one source. In an AIMS audit this arises where the same evidence engages an ISO/IEC 42001 clause, an Annex A control the organization declared, and the organization's own AIMS requirement.

rows.longest_span: the completion and effectiveness of actions should be verified
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 10.2 d) requires the organization to review the effectiveness of any corrective action taken. ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.7 adds that the completion and effectiveness of actions should be verified, and that this verification can be part of a subsequent audit. A finding closed on the strength of a commitment to act, rather than on evidence that action was taken and worked, has not been verified.

rows.longest_span: used as a reference against which objective evidence
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.8 defines audit criteria as the set of requirements used as a reference against which objective evidence is compared - which may include policies, procedures, legal requirements, contractual obligations and standards.

rows.longest_span: the need for action to eliminate the causes
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 10.2 a) requires action to control and correct the nonconformity and deal with the consequences; clause 10.2 b) requires evaluating the need for action to eliminate the causes. Neither term is defined inside ISO/IEC 27001.

rows.longest_span: preparing and distributing the audit report 6 5
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6 sets out the activities of an individual audit in order: initiating the audit (6.2), preparing auditing activities (6.3), conducting auditing activities (6.4), preparing and distributing the audit report (6.5), completing the audit (6.6) and conducting the audit follow-up (6.7). The sequence is guidance, and clause 6.1 notes it can be adapted; what it is not is a checklist that substitutes for judgement about what a particular audit needs.

rows.longest_span: determining the feasibility of the audit 6 2
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.2 covers initiating the audit: establishing contact with the auditee (6.2.2) and determining the feasibility of the audit (6.2.3). Establishing contact confirms authority for the audit, provides information on objectives, scope, methods and team composition, and arranges access. It is where the audit's terms are agreed rather than assumed.

rows.longest_span: consider the intended purpose of the ai systems
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 4.1 requires the organization to consider the intended purpose of the AI systems it develops, provides or uses. Intended purpose is what shapes both the role determination and, later, the impact assessment under 6.1.4, which addresses deployment, intended use and foreseeable misuse. A system whose intended purpose was never recorded leaves both downstream determinations without a basis.

rows.longest_span: potential consequences to the organization individuals and societies
rows.description: Clause 6.1.4 directs the impact assessment outward, to individuals, groups of individuals and societies, rather than inward to the organization. This is the substantive difference from a conventional management-system risk assessment, where consequences are usually scoped to the organization's own objectives. Note that clause 6.1.2 d) 1) does ask the risk analysis to assess potential consequences to the organization, individuals and societies, and its NOTE records that an impact assessment can be used for that purpose.

rows.longest_span: on the basis of education training or experience
rows.description: A job title is not evidence of competence and a headcount is not evidence that competence was determined. Clause 7.2 asks first what competence the work requires and then whether the people doing it hold it, on the basis of education, training or experience, with documented information available as evidence. The common gap is an AIMS that states a competence standard which the personnel records do not evidence.

rows.longest_span: be truthful accurate objective timely clear and complete
rows.description: A finding records what the evidence showed against the criterion. Whether anyone intended, concealed or neglected anything is not something audit evidence establishes, and asserting it converts a factual statement into an allegation the auditor cannot support. ISO 19011:2026 clause 4.3 asks that reporting be truthful, accurate, objective, timely, clear and complete, and attribution of motive fails the objectivity element.

rows.longest_span: assigning responsibility for an individual audit to
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.5 covers assigning responsibility for an individual audit to a team leader, who carries the conduct of that audit.

rows.longest_span: be collected by means of appropriate sampling
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.6 gives the guidance on audit sampling; clause 6.4.7 requires information to be collected by means of appropriate sampling.

rows.longest_span: acceptance of the residual information security risks
rows.description: Clause 6.1.3 f) requires the organization to obtain risk owners approval of the risk treatment plan and their acceptance of the residual information security risks.

rows.longest_span: similar nonconformities exist or could potentially occur
rows.description: Whether a set of findings indicates individual lapses or a failure of the arrangement itself. ISO/IEC 27001 clause 10.2 b) 3) requires the organization to determine whether similar nonconformities exist or could potentially occur.

rows.longest_span: the effectiveness of any corrective action taken
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 10.2 d) requires the effectiveness of any corrective action taken to be reviewed - which requires evidence of the changed arrangement operating, not evidence that it was made.

rows.longest_span: document gives guidance on auditing management systems
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 1 states that the document gives guidance on auditing management systems. It contains 264 instances of should and one of shall, which is boilerplate about ISO patent rights and not an audit requirement. Clause 2 records that there are no normative references in the document. An auditor may therefore write that ISO 19011 recommends, advises or calls for something, and may quote a clause and its modal, but never that ISO 19011 requires or mandates anything.

rows.longest_span: the individual managing the audit programme and
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 7.2 covers determining auditor competence, distinguishing personal behaviour (7.2.2) from knowledge and skills (7.2.3). Clause 5.4.2 addresses the competence of the individual managing the audit programme, and 5.5.4 the selection of audit team members. Clause 7.3 adds that evaluation criteria should be both qualitative and quantitative. All of it is guidance; the organization determines what competence its own programme requires.

rows.longest_span: if they are competent to do so
rows.description: Where the audit team lacks the competence an AI system demands, the available responses are to add a technical expert, to train or pair the auditor, to narrow the audit scope and say so, or to reschedule until competence is available. What is not available is proceeding and writing conclusions the evidence was never understood well enough to support, since ISO 19011:2026 clause 4.2 b) asks auditors to undertake auditing activities only if they are competent to do so.

rows.longest_span: to the audit objectives scope and criteria
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.3.1 covers performing the review of documented information before fieldwork: understanding the management system, gathering information to prepare audit activities and working documents, and forming a view of the extent of documentation relative to the audit objectives, scope and criteria. If what is supplied is inadequate the audit team leader should inform those responsible, and decide whether to continue or to suspend until the matter is resolved.

rows.longest_span: records statements of fact or other information
rows.description: A description of a process is not evidence that the process operates. ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.10 defines audit evidence as records, statements of fact or other information relevant to the audit criteria and verifiable. A statement of fact from an interviewee can be audit evidence; an opinion, an intention or an assurance is not, and the auditor's confidence in the speaker does not convert one into the other.

rows.longest_span: consideration of associated risks and opportunities which
rows.description: Remote is not the lesser option and on-site is not automatically the rigorous one. Documentary evidence, registries and logs are examined equally well from anywhere; the operating environment, physical controls and the observable behaviour of a team may not be. ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.3 asks that the balance of methods be suitably balanced with consideration of associated risks and opportunities, which makes the choice a recorded judgement rather than a default.

rows.longest_span: to achieve the intended results of the
rows.description: Clause 4.1 requires determination of external and internal issues relevant to the organization's purpose and affecting its ability to achieve the intended results of the AI management system. For an AI management system these commonly include applicable regulation, the expectations of affected individuals, the maturity of the technology in use, and dependence on external model or data providers.

rows.longest_span: annex a to verify that no necessary
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 6.1.3 requires the organization to define an AI risk treatment process that selects appropriate treatment options; determines all controls necessary to implement them and compares those controls with Annex A to verify that no necessary control has been omitted; considers the Annex A controls relevant to the chosen options; identifies any additional controls needed beyond Annex A; considers the guidance in Annex B for implementation; and produces a statement of applicability containing the necessary controls with justification for inclusion and exclusion.

rows.longest_span: retain documented information of the results the
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 separates defining the process from performing it. Clause 6.1.4 requires the process to be defined; clause 8.4 requires the organization to perform AI system impact assessments at planned times and when significant changes occur, and to retain documented information of the results. The same split applies to risk: 6.1.2 and 6.1.3 define, 8.2 and 8.3 perform.

rows.longest_span: audit criteria against which conformity is demonstrated
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.18.2 asks that a record of conformity consider a description of or reference to the audit criteria against which conformity is demonstrated, the audit evidence supporting conformity and effectiveness where applicable, and a declaration of conformity where applicable. Clause 6.4.8 adds that where the audit plan specifies it, findings of conformity and of good practice should be recorded with their supporting evidence.

rows.longest_span: should be issued within an agreed period
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.5.2 covers distributing the audit report, which should be issued within an agreed period and to the recipients defined in the audit programme or plan. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.2.2 c) separately requires that the results of audits be reported to relevant managers, which is the requirement a finding about distribution would rest on.

rows.longest_span: similar nonconformities exist or can potentially occur
rows.description: Clause 10.2 b) requires the organization to review the nonconformity, determine its causes, and determine whether similar nonconformities exist or can potentially occur. The third element is the one most often skipped: an organization that has fixed the instance and identified a cause but never asked where else the cause operates has not completed 10.2 b), and the evidence of that omission is in its own corrective action record.

rows.longest_span: extent and boundaries of an audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.6 defines audit scope as the extent and boundaries of an audit, generally including physical and virtual locations, functions, organizational units, activities and processes, and the time period covered.

rows.longest_span: internal audits at planned intervals and
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 requires internal audits at planned intervals and sets no numeric value. The organization determines a defensible interval from process importance and previous results; annual is a choice requiring justification, not a requirement.

rows.longest_span: audit evidence leading to audit findings
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.7 covers managing audit-related records. Clause 6.4.7 requires audit evidence leading to audit findings to be recorded.

rows.longest_span: objectives at relevant functions and levels
rows.description: Clause 6.2 requires objectives at relevant functions and levels, meeting seven stated requirements, and requires the organization to determine five things about how each will be achieved.

rows.longest_span: a description of or reference to
rows.description: Where a finding is combined, each criterion it engages is still named. Annex A.18.3 a) asks for a description of or reference to the audit criteria, and the plural matters: a finding that cites the clause but not the declared control it also breaches leaves part of its own basis unstated and is harder to defend if challenged.

rows.longest_span: the objectives of the audit programme
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 distinguishes the objectives of the audit programme (clause 5.2) from the objectives of an individual audit (clause 5.5.2), and states that the latter should be consistent with the former. The programme spans a set of audits over a time frame and directs where audit effort goes; an individual audit defines what that one audit is to accomplish. Conflating them produces a programme that is a schedule rather than a design.

rows.longest_span: reviewing and improving the audit programme
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.7 addresses reviewing and improving the audit programme. A review considers whether the programme's objectives remain appropriate, what the results across audits show, whether resourcing and competence were adequate, and what should change. The programme is itself subject to improvement, and treating it as fixed is a common weakness an internal auditor can raise about their own function.

rows.longest_span: requirements will be addressed through the
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 4.2 requires the organization to determine the interested parties relevant to the AI management system, their relevant requirements, and which of those requirements will be addressed through the management system. The third element is the one most often missing: identifying a requirement without recording whether the AIMS addresses it leaves the determination incomplete.

rows.longest_span: the organization's own requirements for its
rows.description: Clause 6.1.2 requires the risk assessment process to identify, analyse and evaluate AI risks, which presupposes criteria against which risks are evaluated. The auditor tests the process against the criteria the organization itself established, since clause 9.2.1 makes the organization's own requirements for its AIMS part of the audit criteria alongside the standard.

rows.longest_span: 6 1 3 f requires the
rows.description: Clause 6.1.3 f) requires the statement of applicability to contain the necessary controls and to provide justification for inclusions and exclusions. Both directions need a reason. A statement of applicability that lists included controls without justification, or that marks exclusions with a bare not applicable, has not met the clause even though every row is present.

rows.longest_span: does not recur or occur elsewhere
rows.description: A correction addresses the instance; a corrective action addresses the cause so the instance does not recur or occur elsewhere. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 10.2 a) covers the first and 10.2 b) the second, and they are separate obligations. Completing the missing documentation for one AI system is a correction; establishing why it was missing and whether other systems are affected is the corrective action.

rows.longest_span: the risks and opportunities that
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.3 covers determining and evaluating the risks and opportunities that attach to the audit programme itself - as distinct from the risks the audited system manages.

rows.longest_span: guidance on the competence of
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27007 offers guidance on the competence of ISMS auditors in addition to ISO 19011, covering the information security knowledge an ISMS audit requires.

rows.longest_span: does not reflect their importance
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001's Introduction states that the order in which its requirements are presented does not reflect their importance. Auditing clause by clause in numeric sequence imports a priority the standard disclaims.

rows.longest_span: selecting and determining auditing methods
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.3 covers selecting and determining auditing methods, which may combine on-site and remote activity within a single audit.

rows.longest_span: be appropriate to the organization's
rows.description: Clause 5.2 requires the policy to be appropriate to the organization's purpose, to include objectives or provide the framework for setting them, and to include commitments to satisfy applicable requirements and to continual improvement.

rows.longest_span: consistent valid and comparable results
rows.description: Clause 6.1.2 requires a defined and applied process that establishes risk criteria, produces consistent, valid and comparable results, identifies risks and risk owners, analyses consequences and likelihood, and evaluates against the criteria.

rows.longest_span: 1 requires the organization to
rows.description: Clause 6.1.2 a) 1) requires the organization to establish and maintain risk acceptance criteria, alongside criteria for performing risk assessments.

rows.longest_span: documented information of the results
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 does not require a risk register. Clauses 6.1.2 and 6.1.3 require documented information about the processes; clauses 8.2 and 8.3 require documented information of the results. A register is one way to satisfy this, not the requirement.

rows.longest_span: documented information of external origin
rows.description: Clause 7.5 covers what the ISMS must include (7.5.1), creating and updating (7.5.2), and control (7.5.3), including documented information of external origin the organization determines is necessary.

rows.longest_span: available and suitable for use
rows.description: Clause 7.5.3 requires documented information to be available and suitable for use and adequately protected, addressing distribution, storage, control of changes, and retention and disposition.

rows.longest_span: similar nonconformities exist or could
rows.description: Clause 10.2 b) requires reviewing the nonconformity, determining its causes, and determining whether similar nonconformities exist or could occur. An analysis stopping at the individual who erred has not reached a cause.

rows.longest_span: conducting the audit follow up
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.7 covers conducting the audit follow-up, including verifying completion and effectiveness of actions taken in response to findings.

rows.longest_span: fulfilment of information security objectives
rows.description: Clause 9.3.2 d) 4) requires fulfilment of information security objectives among the performance trends the review considers - a requirement ISO/IEC 42001 does not carry.

rows.longest_span: only on the audit evidence
rows.description: Where independence from the audited activity is not practicable, objectivity is preserved by declared and visible measures rather than by assertion: disclosing the auditor's involvement to the audit client, having a second auditor review the evidence and findings in the affected area, restricting the auditor to evidence others can verify, or assigning that part of the scope to a different member of the audit team. ISO 19011:2026 clause 4.6 asks that findings and conclusions rest only on the audit evidence, which is the test a safeguard has to meet.

rows.longest_span: in a small organization the
rows.description: In a small organization the only person competent to evaluate an AI system is often the person who built or operates it. ISO 19011:2026 anticipates this in clause 4.6 by carving out the case where internal auditors cannot be independent of the activity audited. The response is to name the constraint in the audit plan and record the safeguards applied, not to omit the area from scope or to present the audit as more independent than it was.

rows.longest_span: and can be used as
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42006:2025 specifies additional requirements to ISO/IEC 17021-1 for bodies that audit and certify an AI management system against ISO/IEC 42001. It addresses the competence of certification body personnel, audit time and certification documents, and can be used as accreditation criteria. It applies to the certification body and has no application to a first-party audit, which is why an internal auditor works from ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO 19011 alone.

rows.longest_span: for an ai management system
rows.description: Audit programme objectives are not generic. ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.2 ties them to the audit client's strategic direction and context, which for an AI management system means the AI systems in use, the roles the organization holds toward them, and the interested parties affected. A programme whose objectives could be pasted into any organization has not been derived from context and cannot direct the planning of audits in the way the clause describes.

rows.longest_span: management system conforms to the
rows.description: The criteria for an AIMS internal audit come from ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.2.1, which asks whether the management system conforms to the organization's own requirements for it and to the requirements of the standard, and whether it is effectively implemented and maintained. Both limbs are criteria: an audit that tests only the standard and not the organization's own AIMS requirements has audited half of what clause 9.2.1 names.

rows.longest_span: be based on consideration of
rows.description: The choice between on-site and remote is a question of what the evidence is and where it lives, not of rigour or convenience. A model registry or an event log is examined the same way from any location; an operating environment, a physical control room or the behaviour of a team may not be. ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.3 asks that the balance of methods be based on consideration of associated risks and opportunities, which is a judgement to record rather than a default to apply.

rows.longest_span: monitoring the audit programme and
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.6 covers monitoring the audit programme, and clause 5.5.6 the managing of audit programme results. Monitoring asks whether the programme is being implemented as planned and whether it is achieving its objectives, which is a different question from whether any individual audit was conducted well.

rows.longest_span: the audit can be conducted
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.2.3 addresses determining whether the audit can be conducted at all: whether sufficient and appropriate information is available for planning, whether the auditee will cooperate, and whether adequate time and resources exist. A feasibility problem raised at initiation is a scheduling matter; the same problem discovered during fieldwork has already consumed the audit's time and the auditee's.

rows.longest_span: activities have been carried out
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.6 covers completing the audit, which occurs when the planned activities have been carried out and the report distributed. Clause 6.7 then addresses audit follow-up, which may extend past completion. Documents are retained or disposed of by agreement, and lessons for the audit programme are fed back under clause 5.7.

rows.longest_span: the activities and arrangements for
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.3.2 covers audit planning: the plan describes the activities and arrangements for the audit and provides the basis for agreement among the audit client, audit team and auditee. Its detail should reflect the scope, complexity and the risks and opportunities of the audit. For an AIMS audit the plan is where the specific AI systems, virtual locations and evidence sources are named.

rows.longest_span: providing access to audit information
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.4.5 covers providing access to audit information, and Annex A.16 asks the auditee and audit team to ensure appropriate resources are available when remote methods are used, including agreed remote access protocols, devices and software. Where access is partial, the limit belongs in the audit record: an area the auditor could not reach is an area the audit did not cover, and the report should say so rather than leaving it implied.

rows.longest_span: human resources and their competences
rows.description: An AIMS audit draws on sources a general management-system auditor may not have sampled: documentation of data resources, tooling and computing resources, records of human resources and their competences, AI system technical documentation, event logs, impact assessment outputs and records of system operation and monitoring. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A control families A.4, A.6 and A.7 are where these originate.

rows.longest_span: as part of resource identification
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A.4 covers resources for AI systems, with controls addressing resource documentation and, as part of resource identification, information about data resources, tooling resources, system and computing resources, and human resources and their competences. Annex A.7 covers data for AI systems, including acquisition, quality, provenance and preparation. Where the organization has selected these controls, the documentation they call for is what the auditor samples.

rows.longest_span: 6 1 3 f requires
rows.description: Clause 4.3 does not require the organization to justify exclusions in the way clause 6.1.3 f) requires justification for controls, but an exclusion still has to be consistent with the issues, interested-party requirements and roles that clauses 4.1 and 4.2 produced. An AI system the organization develops, sitting outside a scope that claims to cover development, is an inconsistency the auditor can evidence from the organization's own determinations.

rows.longest_span: to the achievement of the
rows.description: The two processes answer different questions. Clause 6.1.2 assesses risks to the achievement of the organization's AI objectives. Clause 6.1.4 assesses potential consequences for individuals, groups of individuals and societies. They are separately required, separately defined, and directionally linked: 6.1.4 requires its results to be considered in the risk assessment. An organization that has run one process and labelled it both has not met one of the two requirements.

rows.longest_span: documented information required by the
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 7.5.1 requires the AI management system to include the documented information required by the standard and that determined by the organization as necessary for the system's effectiveness. Clause 7.5.2 covers creating and updating it, and 7.5.3 covers its control. A note in 7.5.1 records that the extent can differ between organizations according to size, complexity of processes and competence of persons, so volume is not itself a measure of conformity.

rows.longest_span: non fulfilment of a requirement
rows.description: A nonconformity is the non-fulfilment of a requirement, as ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 3.16 defines it. A should expresses guidance rather than a requirement, so text in the should form cannot be the criterion a nonconformity rests on. The auditor who finds the substance sound but the criterion in the should form records an observation or an opportunity for improvement instead.

rows.longest_span: iso iec 17021 1
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Table 1 sets out the three audit types and their examples. The standard's Introduction states it concentrates on first- and second-party audits and hands third-party certification requirements to ISO/IEC 17021-1.

rows.longest_span: audit programme annex a
rows.description: Two distinct obligations that both speak of planned intervals: clause 9.2 requires an internal audit programme; Annex A 5.35 requires an independent review of the approach. Satisfying one does not satisfy the other.

rows.longest_span: iso iec 17021 1
rows.description: ISO/IEC 17021-1 sets requirements for bodies providing third-party certification of management systems, with ISO/IEC 27006 adding the ISMS-specific requirements. ISO 19011's own Introduction says so.

rows.longest_span: statement of applicability to
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 6.1.3 d) requires the Statement of Applicability to record whether each necessary control is implemented or not. That entry is the organization's claim, and it is what the auditor tests.

rows.longest_span: performed by other organizations
rows.description: Activities performed by other organizations on which the ISMS depends. Clause 4.3 c) names them explicitly, and an undeclared interface is the most common way a scope fails.

rows.longest_span: top management shall demonstrate
rows.description: Clause 5.1 lists eight things top management shall demonstrate, including ensuring the policy and objectives are established and compatible with strategic direction, ensuring resources, and promoting continual improvement.

rows.longest_span: the statement of applicability
rows.description: Clause 6.1.3 requires selecting treatment options, determining all necessary controls, comparing them with Annex A, producing the Statement of Applicability, formulating a treatment plan, and obtaining risk owners approval.

rows.longest_span: objectives criteria and scope
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 9.2.2 a) requires audit criteria and scope; ISO/IEC 42001 requires objectives, criteria and scope. ISO/IEC 27001 reports results to relevant management; ISO/IEC 42001 to relevant managers.

rows.longest_span: against the audit criteria
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.11 defines an audit finding as the result of evaluating collected audit evidence against the audit criteria.

rows.longest_span: iso iec 17021 1
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 uses only the term nonconformity and defines no severity scheme. A major/minor distinction comes from third-party certification practice under ISO/IEC 17021-1. The term nonconformity itself is defined in ISO/IEC 27000.

rows.longest_span: against the audit criteria
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.4.8 covers evaluating audit evidence against the audit criteria to determine findings, including recording conformity as well as nonconformity.

rows.longest_span: feedback from interested parties
rows.description: Clause 9.3.2 lists the inputs the review shall consider, including prior actions, changes in issues and interested party needs, performance feedback, feedback from interested parties, risk assessment results and treatment plan status, and improvement opportunities.

rows.longest_span: based on probability theory
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.6.3 covers sampling designed so that conclusions about the population can be drawn with a stated confidence, which requires a sampling design based on probability theory. It costs more to set up and it supports inference that judgement-based sampling does not. The choice between the two follows from what the audit needs to conclude.

rows.longest_span: for an organization to
rows.description: Because ISO 19011:2026 states no requirements, there is nothing for an organization to conform to and nothing to certify against. It is written for auditors and audit programme managers rather than for the organizations they audit. A claim that an audit programme is compliant with, or certified to, ISO 19011 misdescribes what the document is.

rows.longest_span: the risks to the
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.4.4 covers the resources an audit programme needs, and clause 5.3 names insufficient time, equipment, training and competent auditors among the risks to the programme. Resourcing is where the risk-based approach becomes visible: concentrating auditor days on higher-risk processes necessarily thins coverage elsewhere, and the programme should record that choice rather than leave it implicit.

rows.longest_span: the risk based approach
rows.description: The risk-based approach (4.8) directs effort toward significant matters; the evidence-based approach (4.7) requires that conclusions rest on verifiable evidence drawn from an appropriate sample. Concentrating hours on a high-risk AI system can leave another area sampled too thinly to support any conclusion about it. Nothing in ISO 19011 ranks the two, so the auditor resolves it by judgement and by stating plainly what the audit did and did not cover.

rows.longest_span: is a change in
rows.description: Because obligations attach to roles, a change in role is a change in what the AIMS must cover. An organization that begins offering an internally used system to customers has become a provider; one that starts fine-tuning a model it previously only consumed has taken on development activity. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 6.3 addresses planning of changes, and an audit programme covering an evolving AI estate should expect the role determination to be revisited rather than treated as settled.

rows.longest_span: the organization uses ai
rows.description: A determination applies the developer, provider and user categories to named systems and records why each applies. An assertion says the organization uses AI. The first can be tested against the estate and against clause 4.3 scope; the second cannot be tested at all. Where only the assertion exists, the requirement in clause 4.1 to determine roles has not been met even though the topic has been addressed.

rows.longest_span: the result of the
rows.description: The phrase risk register does not appear anywhere in ISO/IEC 42001:2023. Clause 6.1.2 requires a documented AI risk assessment process; clause 6.1.3 requires a documented risk treatment process and a statement of applicability; clause 6.1.4 requires the result of the impact assessment to be documented. An organization may keep a register and many do, but its absence is not a nonconformity and an auditor who raises one has cited a requirement the standard does not contain.

rows.longest_span: as the result of
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 uses documented information for both what the organization maintains, such as a policy or a process definition, and what it retains as evidence, such as the result of an impact assessment under 6.1.4 or the audit results under 9.2.2. When testing a clause the auditor reads which of the two it asks for: a requirement to define a process is met by the process definition, and a requirement that documented information be available as evidence is met by the record of it having run.

rows.longest_span: clauses 4 to 10
rows.description: In ISO/IEC 42001:2023 a shall is a requirement, a should is guidance and a note is neither. The distinction is structural rather than stylistic: clauses 4 to 10 contain 81 instances of shall and no should at all, while Annex B is almost entirely should. An auditor who preserves the modal in their own writing can be challenged on judgement; one who converts a should into a requirement can be challenged on the text.

rows.longest_span: against the audit criteria
rows.description: A nonconformity statement names the requirement, states the evidence, and asserts the gap between them. ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.11 defines an audit finding as the result of evaluating collected audit evidence against the audit criteria, which is why a statement missing either the criterion or the evidence is not yet a finding.

rows.longest_span: note 2 to entry
rows.description: A note is neither a requirement nor guidance in the sense a should carries, and no finding rests on one. One drafting anomaly is worth knowing rather than turning into an exam point: Note 2 to entry under ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 3.26 contains a shall. Where the statement of applicability is at issue, clause 6.1.3 f) is the requirement text to cite.

rows.longest_span: clauses 4 to 10
rows.description: Before a finding is recorded the auditor identifies the requirement it rests on and confirms the requirement exists in the form claimed. ISO 19011 contains none, so nothing can be found non-conforming to it. Annex A controls apply where declared. Clauses 4 to 10 of ISO/IEC 42001:2023 are stated in shall throughout and apply in full. A finding that cannot name its requirement is withdrawn, not softened.
Requirements determined under clause 4.2 that the ISMS addresses can shape what the programme must give assurance about, particularly where they are contractual or regulatory.
Because ISO 19011 states no requirements, there is nothing to certify against. Claims of being certified to ISO 19011 describe something that does not exist.
ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.4 covers composing the team so that the competence needed for the audit's scope and criteria is present across it.
An externally provided model or API enters the ISMS through the Annex A supplier-relationship controls, making the provider part of what the programme must cover.
ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.2.3 covers determining whether an audit is feasible, including whether the necessary access, cooperation, information and resources are available.

ISO/IEC 27001 clause 9.1 names responsibility for monitoring and for evaluation as things the organization must determine. An arrangement where no one is named does not satisfy the clause even if measurement occurs.
The structural relationship an auditor uses to locate evidence: clause 6 requires the process to be defined; clause 8 requires it to be operated, with the results retained.
The categories an audit programme uses to grade findings. ISO/IEC 27001 defines none, so the scheme is the organization's own declared choice and the auditor applies the scheme in force.

ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.6.2 covers sampling that relies on the auditor's knowledge and experience to select what to examine, targeting items by risk, materiality, complexity or previous findings. It is efficient and it does not support a statistical statement about the population. The auditor who samples this way can say what the examined items showed; they cannot report a rate.

A finding rests on the sample that produced it. If ten of a thousand model cards were examined and three lacked required content, the defensible statement concerns those three and what they indicate; a claim about the other nine hundred and ninety requires a sampling design that supports it. ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.6.1 names non-representativeness as the inherent sampling risk, which is why the sample and its basis belong in the audit record.

The role determination under clause 4.1 is auditable because it produces an output: the AI systems named, a role assigned to each, and the reasoning behind the assignment. The auditor tests whether that output exists and whether it covers the systems actually in use, rather than whether the organization can describe its roles when asked.
